cases.why: The shopper's `q` parameter is spliced straight into the statement text that `sql.raw` hands to Postgres, inside a single-quoted ILIKE literal. A quote in the term ends the literal and the rest of the request becomes SQL — the classic unauthenticated read of any table the storefront role can reach. The ORDER BY fragment genuinely cannot be bound, but the term can be, and the two got composed the same way.

cases.why: The balance is read, checked, and then written back as a value computed in application memory, with no transaction and no predicate on the update. Two requests firing together both read the same balance and both write it minus their own amount, so a 200 EUR card settles two 200 EUR orders and lands at zero rather than overdrawn. The order total is decremented the same way, so the money is really gone.

The debit is a single UPDATE whose WHERE clause re-asserts `balanceCents >= applied` and whose new value is computed by Postgres, inside a transaction with the ledger row and the order total; a loser updates zero rows and is turned away.

That reaches the cloud metadata endpoint, anything on the pod network, and `file:`-adjacent internal services — a request-forgery read primitive with the response handed straight back. cases.why: It resolves the same attacker-controlled rest parameter against a base directory, which is the shape that usually goes wrong — but it then proves the resolved absolute path is the base itself or sits beneath `base + path.sep` before touching the filesystem. Checking after resolution is what makes it correct: `..`, encoded separators and absolute keys have all collapsed by then.
